chapter_intro_summary: The chapter starts from an assistant that can interpret a photograph, read signs, or first transcribe a spoken question. These require different clues. It builds on an already trained image/text base, prepares suitable demonstrations, updates a small part of its weights, and evaluates each ability. It positions chapter 19 as a smaller component-learning exercise that need not be personally trained first. The introduction separates CPU teaching snippets from the finished-model trial and GPU retraining, and previews the chapter sequence. I read this introduction for context only; I did not review §20.1.
reader_summary: The lesson answers why a training conversation can contain both a question and its answer without making the model learn to repeat the question. Inputs remain readable context; a separate aligned target sequence chooses which next-item predictions contribute directly to the cost. In the small Q/A example the assistant boundary predicts A and A predicts the ending, so six input positions produce only two scored targets. Full image/text data require their base model’s processor and template, and truncation must preserve the intended answer and ending. The quoted training totals count encoded targets rather than characters. I could predict and check the A-to-AB exercise after reading the two explicit masking/alignment prerequisites.

background_and_links.details: The classroom-question analogy supplies the motivation: seeing a question is different from being asked to reproduce it as an answer. The introduction gives the demonstration-fine-tuning context. I actually opened only the explicitly linked §§7.3–7.4, which supplied the needed masking and next-item alignment background. I did not need chapter 19 or further linked chapters to follow the example.

terminology.details: The prose defines the mask as scoring marks, expands SFT and states what supervised fine-tuning does, distinguishes input IDs from target -100, and explains processor/template duties in concrete terms. The prerequisite explains True/False tensors, sum/item, nonzero and next-item targets. Qwen reads as the name of the full model used for image/text data; its architecture is not required by this toy example. The single unexplained transition phrase 「修正分支」 is recorded as a nonblocking wording suggestion.

examples.details: For Q/A the six input positions are start, user, Q, user-end, assistant boundary, and A. The assistant boundary predicts A, and A predicts the final end. Thus the two valid targets differ from the six readable inputs. The section explicitly warns that these six positions do not describe the full Qwen image input. I can interpret 2,077 as training questions, 39,436 as encoded scored target positions including the final assistant answer and template suffix, and 78,872 as twice that count for two passes. Those are position counts, not Chinese character counts or independent answers. I did not replicate those earlier training counts.

program_explanation.details: render_chat takes two role/content messages and returns input x and aligned target y. active = y != -100 selects targets that directly count toward the cost. active.nonzero()[0].item() gives the first selected position, len(x) counts input positions, active.sum().item() counts selected targets, and y[active].tolist() shows their token IDs. §7.4 supplies the specific Q=89, A=73, and end=2 ID mapping, separate from index 4. My exact-fence CPU run printed 6 inputs, 2 scored targets, first index 4, and IDs [73, 2]. An additional inspection probe printed the complete x/y lists and confirmed Q remains present.

exercise.details: I saved the prediction before running: replacing answer A with AB adds one answer byte, so the input grows from 6 to 7 positions and the scored targets from 2 to 3; first scored index stays 4 and target IDs become [73, 74, 2]. The exercise run matched these values. The separate x/y inspection showed question ID 89 retained at x[2] in both variants. No model download, GPU use or training was involved.

Arrows show assistant→A and A→end. The explicit note says this is not the full image/text-model sequence length. At both 720 px and 358 px the Chinese labels, arrows and note were readable, with no clipping. The input Q remains visibly present even though its row is not scored.

I saw the full original BOS user Q EOS assistant A EOS sequence and a table separating position, input X, and next-item Y. Grey rows 0–3 show ignored -100 targets. Green row 4 maps assistant ID 4 to A ID 73; green row 5 maps A ID 73 to EOS ID 2. The bottom line explicitly distinguishes predicting A at position 4 from position 5. Both viewed sizes were readable; I found no overlapping labels or cropped content.
